facts.text: On this date in 1886, the Statue of Liberty was dedicated — but France gave only the statue itself. The pedestal was America's responsibility, funded largely through 120,000 small donations after wealthy patrons refused to pay.

On this date in 1962, Khrushchev announced Soviet missiles would leave Cuba, ending the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange. The US secretly agreed to remove its own missiles from Turkey — a concession kept hidden from the public for decades.

Mongolia has more horses than people. With roughly 4.3 million residents and over 5 million horses, it is the only country on Earth where the livestock-to-human ratio tips so decisively in the animals' favor.

Tokyo is not Japan's capital by law. No Japanese legislation formally designates any city as the capital — Tokyo assumed the role by convention when the Emperor moved there in 1869, and the legal ambiguity has never been resolved.

More people live inside a circle drawn around Dhaka, Bangladesh than inside a circle of the same size drawn around any other point on Earth. The density of South Asia's river delta cities makes the math almost unbelievable.
On this day in 1929, the Dow fell 13% — Black Tuesday. The crash wiped out $14 billion in a single session, the equivalent of roughly $260 billion today.
On October 28, 2008, the Dow surged 889 points, its biggest single-day point gain at the time. It came in the middle of the worst financial crisis since the Depression.
The NYSE's famously chaotic trading floor employs fewer than 500 people today. In its 1980s peak, over 5,000 worked there daily.
Saudi Aramco briefly hit a $2.4 trillion valuation in 2022 — larger than the entire GDP of Italy, which has 60 million people and centuries of industrial history.
The U.S. penny costs 3.7 cents to produce. The government has lost money minting its cheapest coin every year since 2006.

On this date in 1962, Khrushchev announced Soviet missiles would leave Cuba — a decision made while Earth was roughly 8 light-minutes from the Sun, a distance light crosses in the time it took to read this.
On October 28, 1965, the Gateway Arch was completed. Its height and base width are identical at 630 feet — a catenary curve so precise it was calculated before reliable computers existed.
Your bones are not static scaffolding. The entire human skeleton replaces itself every decade, with osteoclasts dissolving old bone while osteoblasts rebuild it, continuously and silently.
A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. A teaspoon of its material would weigh roughly a billion tons on Earth.
Quantum entanglement allows two particles to share a state across any distance, but the correlation appears instantaneously — faster than light, yet useless for sending information.
On this day in 1886, the Statue of Liberty was dedicated — making her older than the Eiffel Tower, the zipper, and the diesel engine.
Oxford University was already 300 years old when the Aztec Empire was founded. Harvard still hadn't been imagined.
On this day in 1962, Khrushchev announced Soviet missiles would leave Cuba — the closest humanity has come to nuclear war ended with a letter and a phone call.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. Egypt's own history dwarfed her.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — before the American Civil War, before the telephone, and 137 years before the Post-it note.
Sonder (n.): the sudden awareness that every stranger has a life as vivid and complex as your own. Coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, 2012 — now widely adopted as if ancient.
Mamihlapinatapai: a Yaghan word for the shared, wordless look between two people who both want something but won't initiate. Once called the world's most succinct word by Guinness.
On this date in 1886, the Statue of Liberty was dedicated — its torch embodying the French word 'lumière,' light, echoing the Enlightenment ideal that liberty itself illuminates.
Saudade (n.): a Portuguese ache for something loved and lost, or never had. Untranslatable by design — the Portuguese argue no other language has felt loss the same way.
On Oct 28, 1955, Bill Gates was born. His surname descends from the Old Norse 'gat,' meaning a gap or opening in a fence — an entrance, aptly enough, to everything that followed.

On this date in 2008, Satoshi Nakamoto published the Bitcoin whitepaper to a cryptography mailing list. Nine people replied. None realized they were reading the founding document of a $1 trillion asset class.
On Oct 28, 2021, Facebook rebranded to Meta — triggering a 900% spike in transactions for unrelated token $META within 48 hours, a textbook case of ticker confusion arbitrage.

Bitcoin's 21 million supply cap is never explicitly stated in the whitepaper. It emerges implicitly from the halving schedule coded into the protocol — a design choice Satoshi never publicly explained.

The Ethereum genesis block, mined July 30, 2015, contained a hidden message in its extra data field: 'dao-hard-fork'. That field was actually empty — the message people cite is from a later block, a persistent myth.

CryptoKitties didn't just clog Ethereum in 2017 — it exposed that the network had no congestion pricing. Every subsequent EIP addressing fee markets, including EIP-1559, traces its urgency to those cartoon cats.

On this date in 2003, Geoffrey Hinton published the paper introducing Contrastive Divergence, the training trick that quietly made deep Boltzmann machines viable and set the stage for the 2006 deep learning revival.

On this date in 2011, Apple shipped Siri in iOS 5 — the first mass-market neural-network voice assistant. It ran almost entirely on Apple's servers; the phone itself was just a microphone and a screen.

AlphaFold 2 predicted structures for over 200 million proteins — essentially the entire known universe of protein sequences — in roughly a year. Experimental X-ray crystallography would have taken longer than the age of the Earth.
The original GPT-3 training run consumed an estimated 3.14 × 10²³ FLOPs. At peak A100 throughput, a single GPU would need roughly 355 years to replicate it alone.

RLHF — the technique that turned raw language models into instruction-following assistants — was first applied to summarization in a 2020 OpenAI paper. The core idea borrows directly from 1990s animal-training research on reward shaping.
